chapter.title: A photo, not a film

cards.body: A balance sheet is a photo of the house taken at midnight on one day. It shows the house, the car in the drive, the cash in the kitchen drawer and the mortgage letter on the table, all frozen. It does not show the year of rent you collected or the roof you fixed in March: **it only shows what was there the moment the shutter clicked.**
cards.simpler: Think of a balance sheet as a photo of a house, taken at midnight on one day. You see the house, the car outside, the cash in the kitchen drawer and the mortgage letter on the table. Everything is frozen. You do not see the rent collected over the year or the roof fixed in March. **It only shows what was there the moment the shutter clicked.**

cards.prompt: Priya photographs her flat at midnight on 31 December. On 2 January she buys a sofa for 600. What does the 31 December photo show?

options.text: The sofa, because the photo covers the whole year
No sofa, because the photo only knows that one midnight
The sofa, with a note saying it arrived later

whyNot.a: That's a film covering a stretch of time, not a photo: a balance sheet only knows one moment.
whyNot.c: That's wishful: the photo cannot see 2 January. Anything bought after the date is simply absent.

cards.reteach: A balance sheet carries one date. Whatever the company owned and owed at the end of that day is on it. Anything that happened the day after is not there, with or without a note.

cards.title: Where the date sits
cards.body:
Look at the very top of any balance sheet. Under the title you will see words like *as at 31 December 2025* or *as of 30 June*. That tiny phrase is the whole point: **the sheet describes one single day.**

The income statement, the other main report, says *for the year ended 31 December*. 'For the year' means a stretch of time, a film. 'As at' means a moment, a photo.

So a balance sheet can tell you the cash in the bank on that day. It cannot tell you how much the company earned getting there.
cards.simpler:
Look at the top of any balance sheet. Under the title you will see *as at 31 December 2025* or *as of 30 June*. That small phrase matters most: **the sheet describes one single day.**

The other main report, the income statement, says *for the year ended*. That covers a stretch of time, like a film. *As at* means one moment, like a photo.

So a balance sheet can tell you the cash in the bank that day. It cannot tell you how much the company earned to get there.

cards.title: Nadia and the oven
cards.body: Nadia runs a bakery. Her balance sheet says cash 2,000 as at 31 December. You say, 'Only 2,000? Rough year.' She laughs. On 30 December she paid 40,000 for a second oven. The year was her best ever; **the photo just caught her the morning after a big shop.** Two days earlier, the cash line would have read 42,000 and you'd have called her rich.
cards.simpler: Nadia runs a bakery. Her balance sheet says cash 2,000 as at 31 December. You say, 'Only 2,000? Hard year.' She laughs. On 30 December she paid 40,000 for a second oven. It was her best year ever. **The photo just caught her the morning after a big shop.** Two days earlier the cash line would have said 42,000, and you would have called her rich.

cards.prompt: A friend hands you two reports from the same shop. One says 'as at 31 March 2025'. The other says 'for the year ended 31 March 2025'. Which is the balance sheet?

options.text: The first, because 'as at' names one day
The second, because a whole year is more useful
Both, since they carry the same date

whyNot.b: That's the income statement: 'for the year ended' covers a stretch of time, a film, not a photo.
whyNot.c: They share a date but not a job: one freezes a moment, the other adds up twelve months.

cards.reteach: The clue is the small word before the date. 'As at' or 'as of' means one day, so it is the balance sheet. 'For the year ended' means a period, so it is the income statement.

cards.title: Why two dates sit side by side
cards.body:
Most published balance sheets show two columns: this year's date and the same date last year. Two photos, one year apart. **The gap between the two columns is the story a single photo cannot tell.**

If cash was 50,000 last year and 10,000 now, something happened. The sheet will not say what. Maybe a new oven, maybe a bad year, maybe a loan paid off. Your job is to notice the jump and go looking.

Also check the day itself. A toy shop photographed on 20 December, stockroom full for the rush, looks nothing like the same shop on 15 January.
cards.simpler:
Most balance sheets show two columns. One is this year's date. The other is the same date last year. Two photos, one year apart. **The gap between the two columns is the story a single photo cannot tell.**

If cash was 50,000 last year and 10,000 now, something happened. The sheet will not say what. Maybe a new oven, a bad year, or a loan paid off. Notice the jump, then go looking.

Check the day too. A toy shop on 20 December, shelves full for the rush, looks nothing like the same shop on 15 January.

cards.body: Tom sees *cash 10,000* on a sheet dated 31 December and tells his brother, 'They only brought in 10,000 all year.' But the sheet never said how much came in. Ten thousand is what sat in the bank at midnight on one day; far more may have flowed in and out before that. Spot the slip: the words 'brought in', 'made' or 'earned' pointed at a balance sheet mean someone has **mistaken the photo for the film.**
cards.simpler: Tom sees *cash 10,000* on a sheet dated 31 December. He tells his brother, 'They only brought in 10,000 all year.' But the sheet never said how much came in. Ten thousand is what sat in the bank at midnight on one day. Far more may have come and gone before that. Words like 'brought in', 'made' or 'earned', aimed at a balance sheet, mean someone has **mistaken the photo for the film.**

cards.prompt: Which question can a balance sheet answer on its own?

options.text: How much did the company earn between January and December?
How much cash did it hold on 31 December?
How much did it spend on wages this year?

whyNot.a: That's the income statement's job: earning happens over a stretch of time, and a photo cannot show a stretch.
whyNot.c: That's spending over a year, a film question. The balance sheet only shows what was left on the day.

cards.reteach: If the question contains 'during', 'this year' or 'between', it is a film question and needs the income statement. If it asks about one date, it is a photo question and the balance sheet can answer it.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A balance sheet is **a photo taken on one day**, so find the words *as at* and the date before you read anything else. It shows what was there at that moment, never how much was earned getting there; for that you need the film, the income statement.
cards.simpler: A balance sheet is **a photo taken on one day.** So find the words *as at* and the date before you read anything else. The sheet shows what was there at that moment. It never shows how much was earned getting there. For that, you need the film, which is the income statement.

cards.body: Open any big company's annual report online, find the balance sheet, and look for 'as at' or 'as of'. **Say the date out loud.** Then find the two columns and spot one line that jumped.
cards.simpler: Open any big company's annual report online. Find the balance sheet. Look for the words 'as at' or 'as of'. **Say the date out loud.** Then find the two columns, this year and last year, and spot one line that jumped between them.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now point to the date on any balance sheet, say which single day it describes, and explain why it cannot tell you what the company earned.
